papers.title: The Theory of Dyadic Morality: Reinventing Moral Judgment by Redefining Harm
papers.abstract_snippet: Comprehensive presentation of TDM: acts are condemned proportional to norm violations, negative affect, and perceived harm. Harm is dyadic—an intentional agent causing damage to a vulnerable patient (A→P). Predicts dyadic comparison (harm→immorality) and dyadic completion (immorality→harm), forming the 'dyadic loop.'

papers.title: Mind Perception Is the Essence of Morality
papers.authors: Kurt Gray, Liane Young, Adam Waytz
papers.abstract_snippet: Argues moral judgment is rooted in perceiving two complementary minds—an intentional moral agent and a suffering moral patient (the moral dyad). Dimensions of mind perception (agency and experience) map onto moral types. Deficits in mind perception correspond to difficulties with moral judgment.

papers.title: The Moral Dyad: A Fundamental Template Unifying Moral Judgment
papers.authors: Kurt Gray, Adam Waytz, Liane Young
papers.abstract_snippet: Proposes that the diversity of moral judgment is underlain by the moral dyad—a psychological template of two perceived minds (moral agent and moral patient). All moral transgressions are fundamentally understood as agency plus experienced suffering, even ostensibly harmless purity violations.

papers.title: Moral Typecasting: Divergent Perceptions of Moral Agents and Moral Patients
papers.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
papers.abstract_snippet: Introduces moral typecasting through 7 studies: a person perceived as a moral agent is less likely to be perceived as a moral patient, and vice versa. Good- and evil-doers were perceived as less vulnerable to harm. Stems from the dyadic nature of morality.

papers.title: The Myth of Harmless Wrongs in Moral Cognition: Automatic Dyadic Completion From Sin to Suffering
papers.authors: Kurt Gray, Chelsea Schein, Adrian F. Ward
papers.abstract_snippet: Five studies reveal dyadic completion occurs automatically and implicitly: ostensibly harmless wrongs are perceived to have victims, activate concepts of harm, and increase perceptions of suffering. Victimless wrongs are psychologically incomplete—the mind perceives victims even when objectively absent.

papers.title: The Unifying Moral Dyad: Liberals and Conservatives Share the Same Harm-Based Moral Template
papers.abstract_snippet: Argues that moral cognition in both liberals and conservatives is rooted in a harm-based template. Ratings of immorality of purity and loyalty violations were more strongly associated with harm than with their fellow binding content. Moral judgment occurs via dyadic comparison with a prototype of harm.

papers.title: The Affective Harm Account (AHA) of Moral Judgment: Reconciling Cognition and Affect, Dyadic Morality and Disgust, Harm and Purity
papers.authors: Kurt Gray, Chelsea Schein, et al.
papers.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology
papers.abstract_snippet: Reconciles harm vs. affect debate via the AHA: perceived harm is consistently relevant across all scenarios (supporting TDM), while affective appraisals are especially relevant in unusual purity scenarios. Tested with double-blind propranolol pharmacological experiment. Visceral arousal does not directly impact moral judgment.

papers.title: Morality Takes Two: Dyadic Morality and Mind Perception
papers.venue: Chapter in The Social Psychology of Morality (Mikulincer & Shaver, Eds.)
papers.abstract_snippet: Foundational chapter linking dyadic morality to mind perception: moral judgment requires perceiving two minds—an intentional agent and a suffering patient. Dimensions of mind perception (agency and experience) map onto moral types (agents and patients).

papers.title: The Puzzle of Wrongless Harms: Some Potential Concerns for Dyadic Morality and Related Accounts
papers.authors: Edward B. Royzman, Samuel H. Borislow
papers.abstract_snippet: Challenges TDM by presenting 'wrongless harms'—behaviors judged as intended, self-serving, and foreseeably harmful yet not immoral (e.g., boxing, breaking up). Argues moral cognition is too complex to be reduced to a template. Requires further refinement of dyadic morality's predictions.

papers.title: Modeling Morality in 3-D: Decision-Making, Judgment, and Inference
papers.abstract_snippet: Computational framework for moral cognition across three dimensions: decision-making, judgment, and inference. Integrates harm aversion as moral sentiment with Bayesian reinforcement learning models. Different dimensions of moral cognition built upon basic utility computations trading off costs and benefits.

papers.title: A Conceptual and Computational Model of Moral Decision Making in Human and Artificial Agents
papers.authors: Wendell Wallach, Stan Franklin, Colin Allen
papers.abstract_snippet: Presents a computational model based on the LIDA framework for implementing moral decision-making in AI. Describes how to implement reflexive value-laden responses while explaining how responses can be reinforced or inhibited through learning, deliberation, and metacognition.

papers.title: Large Language Models Show Amplified Cognitive Biases in Moral Decision-Making
papers.abstract_snippet: LLMs exhibit distinct patterns of moral judgment varying substantially from human evaluations. LLMs show moderate to high self-consistency but low inter-model agreement, with yes-no bias and omission bias in moral dilemmas. Fine-tuning for chatbot applications can amplify biases.

papers.title: Dimensions of Moral Emotions
papers.abstract_snippet: Examines moral emotions through the lens of moral typecasting and the dyadic framework. Connects dimensions of emotional experience to the agent-patient distinction in moral psychology.
